anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.text:
## (1) First message

The framing holds: I checked `src/export/csv.ts:40`, where the serializer builds its columns (`title`, `status`, `owner`) from the reports table's own definitions, and the draft's finding that the reports page renders that table with no export action. The work is therefore wiring an existing serializer to a new button, not building an exporter. I traced no caller of `csv.ts` other than the column list, and I have not read the reports page's data path, so the next message treats both as unverified. I've recorded `Framing: kept` in the draft. I'm also assuming the export covers every row of the report under its current filters, not just the visible page, because the ticket's 10k-row criterion only makes sense under that reading.

Where should the Export CSV button sit on the reports page? A) beside the report title B) in a toolbar directly above the table C) inside an existing page-level actions menu D) other - name it. Recommendation: A - the button belongs to the report as a whole, and the title area is the most visible spot that doesn't imply a per-page or per-selection export.

---

## (2) Approaches message

First, the premises behind the design.

- **Owner column: supported.** The ticket's owner-column row is backed by `src/export/csv.ts:40`, whose column list already contains `owner`. Any approach that reuses that list satisfies the row as written.
- **No export action: not independently verified.** The draft says the reports page has no export action, but I haven't seen the page code, so this is the gather draft's finding only.
- **Serializer and paging: unverified.** The draft says "all ticket rows match the table contract," and the evidence covers only the column list. I've seen nothing of the serializer's function signature or of any paging mechanism. Your plan to reuse the existing paging therefore rests on something I can't yet cite.
- **10k rows under 60s: unverified.** Nothing in the draft or fixture measures export time. Whether that row is cheap or costly depends on how the rows are fetched.

None of this blocks the design. The serializer's entry point and the paging mechanism go into Open Questions for the plan to confirm.

Approaches. The axis is where the full row set gets assembled.

**Recommended - reuse-only, client-side.** The button pages through the report's existing data source and feeds every page to the existing CSV serializer in the browser. It then triggers a download. There is no new construct, just a button handler composing what exists. It meets the owner-column row for free, and the 10k-row timing is likely fine if each page fetch is reasonably fast.
`Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts:40 - the export columns stay derived from the table's column definitions, one source of truth.`

**Server-side streaming endpoint.** This drops the ask's implicit assumption that the export runs where the table renders. A new endpoint streams the CSV using the same column definitions, and the button becomes a plain download link. It decouples export time from browser memory and per-request round trips, which makes the 60s bound easier to guarantee at larger sizes. The cost is a new server entrypoint and a second consumer of the column list across a process boundary.
`Pattern: reuses the src/export/csv.ts:40 columns but adds a new export boundary beside the client-side serializer; justified only if the client path can't meet the timing row.`

**Export only the loaded page.** This one is not viable. It would mean serializing just the rows currently rendered, with no paging, and it can't produce a 10k-row export at all, so it fails an in-scope criterion.

The client-side approach would flip to the server endpoint if the plan finds that paging through 10k rows takes more than about 60s. That would happen if the page size is capped small or each page fetch is slow.

Which approach should the spec carry? A) reuse-only: client-side paging into the existing serializer B) server-side streaming endpoint C) other - name it. Recommendation: A - it adds no new boundary and keeps the column list's single owner. The server endpoint stays the fallback if the timing row can't be met.

---

*(Next message, after your reply "Reuse the existing CSV serializer and paging … can we drop that row?")*

Recorded: approach A, client-side reuse. You've raised dropping a ticket row, so here is that decision explicitly.

The row is "The export of a 10k-row report completes in under 60s." What should the spec do with it? A) in-scope - the reuse approach is built to meet it, and the plan includes a timing check against a 10k-row report B) deviates: the spec ships without a timing guarantee, and you state why C) deferred: moved to a named tracker issue or spec D) repair the ticket - `/skill:shape-ticket acme/widgets#77` with this row and the evidence that it exceeds the sprint's needs. Recommendation: A - the approach you chose likely meets 60s already, so keeping the row costs one measurement rather than new work. If the target is genuinely wrong for the product, D fixes it at the source rather than leaving the spec diverging from the ticket.

github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol.text:
## 1. First message to the user

The supplied column-contract check supports the framing: `src/export/csv.ts:40` includes `title`, `status`, and `owner`, so the requested owner column does not require changing that definition.

The draft’s broader claim that all ticket rows match the implementation is not established. The fixture does not show the reports-page action, CSV serializer, paging callers, or the data path from report fetching through serialization to download. It also provides no evidence for the 10k-row timing requirement. With tools prohibited, I cannot verify those traces or check additional code, documentation, tracker discussion, or existing export functionality. I will treat reuse of the existing serializer and paging as your recorded implementation decision, with their suitability still to be verified.

I’ll place the button beside the report title, as recorded. Your request to drop the performance row needs an explicit scope decision because it changes a verbatim acceptance criterion in `acme/widgets#77`.

**How should we disposition “The export of a 10k-row report completes in under 60s”?**

A) **in-scope** — retain the requirement and verify it using a defined 10k-row fixture and test environment.  
B) **deviates: remove the 10k-row under-60s requirement from this sprint** — ship the export without that performance guarantee.  
C) **deferred: `docs/specs/reports-csv-performance.md`** — retain the requirement as follow-up work documented at that proposed destination.  
D) **repair the ticket** — `/skill:shape-ticket acme/widgets#77` to revise this row based on your stated sprint scope.

**Recommendation: A — the ticket explicitly requires this result, and no supplied code or measurement shows it is infeasible; retain it unless you explicitly choose a scope change.**

## 2. Approaches message

I recommend **reusing the existing CSV serializer and paging**, honoring your recorded implementation choice. The button goes beside the report title.

The owner field is supported by `src/export/csv.ts:40`. The reports page’s lack of an export action comes from the gather draft, not supplied page code. The serializer and paging interfaces, whether they preserve owner values across every page, and the 10k-row runtime remain unverified because their implementations were not provided and tool lookups are prohibited. Nothing supplied disproves the export request, but the draft’s claim of complete contract alignment needs that narrower reading.

The recorded request to drop the timing row is not yet a completed scope-cut decision. These approaches therefore retain it provisionally; neither silently removes it.

The useful design axis is **whole-report buffering versus incremental output**, not introducing another serializer.

### Approach 1: Minimal reuse, with whole-report serialization — recommended

Connect the button to the existing paging path, collect the report rows, and pass them through the existing serializer. Reuse the shared column definition, provided inspection confirms that it is the serializer’s owning contract.

This is the smallest integration and avoids a new export abstraction. Its trade-off is memory consumption and potentially delayed feedback while fetching and serializing the entire report. Error handling should prevent an incomplete download from appearing successful.

**Pattern:** Follows the shared-column contract visible at `src/export/csv.ts:40`; reuse of the serializer and paging follows your recorded choice, but their integration points still require inspection.

### Approach 2: Reuse paging and serialization, with incremental output

Fetch pages through the existing paging path and serialize/write them incrementally, emitting the header once. This drops the design assumption that the complete report must be held in memory before export.

It can bound memory usage and permit progress reporting, but adds output-lifecycle complexity: ordering, cancellation, write failures, and partial-file handling. Its viability depends on the existing serializer supporting page-wise output—or being safely adaptable without creating a second CSV implementation—and an available download sink.

**Pattern:** Preserves the column contract at `src/export/csv.ts:40` rather than introducing parallel field definitions; incremental serializer and download support are unverified, not established repository conventions.

The reuse-only candidate is Approach 1. The assumption-dropping candidate is Approach 2; a separate server or background-job export is not justified by the supplied evidence.

I would switch from Approach 1 to Approach 2 if inspection or a representative 10k-row measurement shows that whole-report buffering cannot meet the retained timing requirement or acceptable memory usage, and incremental output is supported.
